name: Crosswind
seoDesc: Crosswind: work out crosswind component from the headwind component. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Crosswind calculator returns crosswind component from the 3 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Crosswind calculator work?
sections.html:
The Crosswind calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports crosswind component in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the headwind component.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Crosswind calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Crosswind component=wind speed × (the sine of ((1 ÷ 180) × PI × (((the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) > 180) ? ( (((runway number < wind direction) ? ( A ) : ( B ))) ) : ( the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) )))))
Wind speed=headwind component ÷ (the cosine of ((1 ÷ 180) × PI × (((the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) > 180) ? ( (((runway number < wind direction) ? ( A ) : ( B ))) ) : ( the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) )))))
Tailwind component=-wind speed × (the cosine of ((1 ÷ 180) × PI × (((the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) > 180) ? ( (((runway number < wind direction) ? ( A ) : ( B ))) ) : ( the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction) )))))
Wind direction=-A + runway number + 360
Runway number=-B + wind direction + 360
C=the absolute value of (runway number − wind direction)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Crosswind calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the headwind component — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Crosswind calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns crosswind component, derived from the headwind component. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Crosswind calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the headwind component, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter wind direction in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Wind direction opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Crosswind calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
